title: The periodic table
lede: The periodic table is a map. Once you can read it, you can predict how elements behave.

sections.md:
## How it's arranged
Elements are ordered by **atomic number** (protons), left to right, top to bottom.

- **Rows (periods):** each row adds a new layer (shell) of electrons.
- **Columns (groups):** elements in a column have the same number of outer electrons, so they behave alike.

## Neighborhoods
| Region | Examples | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Group 1: alkali metals | sodium, potassium | very reactive, 1 outer electron |
| Group 17: halogens | chlorine, fluorine | very reactive, want 1 more electron |
| Group 18: noble gases | helium, neon | stable, barely react |
| Metals (left and middle) | iron, copper | shiny, conduct electricity |
| Nonmetals (upper right) | oxygen, carbon | poor conductors |

sections.title: Predict a reaction
sections.problem: Sodium (group 1) and chlorine (group 17) meet. What happens?
steps: Sodium has 1 outer electron it easily gives up.
Sodium hands its electron to chlorine.

sections.label: Mendeleev's bet
sections.md: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged his 1869 table by patterns and left gaps for elements nobody had found yet. He predicted their properties, and when gallium and germanium were discovered, they matched. A good model makes predictions.
